title: Behavioral Finance
intro: Standard finance assumes investors are rational. Behavioral finance studies how real people decide, and finds systematic, predictable errors. Knowing them won't make you immune, but it lets you build habits and rules that stop them costing you money.

blocks.text: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's prospect theory (1979) describes how people actually weigh risky choices. We judge outcomes as gains or losses from a reference point (often the price we paid), not as final wealth; we are risk-averse for gains but risk-seeking to avoid a sure loss; and losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains please (loss aversion). We also overweight small probabilities, which is why both lottery tickets and insurance against rare events sell well. Kahneman received the 2002 Nobel memorial prize for this work; Richard Thaler received it in 2017 for applying such ideas to economics.

items: Disposition effect: selling winners too early and holding losers too long, hoping to 'get back to even' (Shefrin and Statman 1985; Odean 1998 found the winners investors sold went on to beat the losers they kept). The price you paid is irrelevant to whether a stock is a good holding now.

Overconfidence: most people rate themselves above-average investors. Barber and Odean (2000) found that the US households who traded most earned about 11.4% a year against 17.9% for the market (1991-96); trading costs and poor timing ate the difference. Men traded about 45% more than women and earned less as a result (2001).
Herding and FOMO: buying what everyone else is buying, especially after big rises: tulips, the 1720 South Sea bubble, the dot-com boom, meme stocks.
Recency bias and extrapolation: expecting recent returns to continue. Fund flows chase past performance, which is why investors' money-weighted returns trail their funds' time-weighted returns.
Anchoring: fixating on an arbitrary number, such as a stock's 52-week high or the price you paid.
Confirmation bias: seeking information that supports what you already believe. Write down the case against every investment you make.
Mental accounting: treating money differently by its source or label (a 'house money' windfall gambled freely, a high-interest card balance carried while cash sits in savings).
Home and familiarity bias: overweighting your own country, region or employer.
Hindsight bias: 'it was obvious' after the fact, which inflates confidence in forecasting the next event.
Narrative fallacy: a good story about a company or technology is not the same as a good investment at today's price.
Myopic loss aversion (Benartzi and Thaler 1995): checking a portfolio often means seeing more losses, which makes stocks feel riskier than they are over the investor's real horizon. Check less often.
Status quo bias and inertia: sticking with defaults, which is harmful when the default is cash and helpful when it is a good automatic plan.

blocks.text: Biases matter for prices only if rational traders can't correct them. Limits to arbitrage (Shleifer and Vishny 1997) explain why mispricings can persist: betting against a bubble takes capital, can lose money for years, and may be impossible to short. 'Markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent' is attributed to Keynes. Hyman Minsky's financial instability hypothesis adds that stability itself breeds risk-taking and leverage, which ends in a crash (a 'Minsky moment').

items: Automate: contribute automatically every month; use target-date or balanced funds or automatic rebalancing. Thaler and Benartzi's 'Save More Tomorrow' plan (2004), committing future raises to savings, raised savings rates from about 3.5% to 13.6% over four years.
Write the plan down (an investment policy statement) and pre-commit to rebalancing rather than reacting.
Check less often. Quarterly is plenty for a long-term portfolio.
Keep a journal of each decision, why you made it, and what would prove you wrong.
Use a checklist before buying anything: what is it, what does it cost, what could go wrong, how does it fit?
Separate a small 'play' account if you enjoy picking stocks, sized so its result doesn't matter.
Ask what an outsider would advise a friend in your position.

blocks.title: Spot the bias
blocks.text: An investor bought a stock at \$80; it is now \$55. They say: 'I'll sell once it gets back to \$80, so I don't lose money.' Which biases are at work, and what is the better question?
solution: Anchoring on the purchase price and the disposition effect (loss aversion). The \$25 loss has already happened whether or not they sell. The right question is: if I had \$55 in cash today, would I buy this stock? If not, sell it (and in a taxable account the loss may even reduce tax).

blocks.title: The cost of chasing
blocks.text: A fund returned 10% a year for 10 years (time-weighted). Most investors put their money in after its best years and withdrew after its worst. Will their average return (money-weighted) be above or below 10%?
solution: Below. Buying after strong periods and selling after weak ones means more money is invested during the weaker stretches. Morningstar's studies of this gap have found investors earning around a point a year less than their funds on average.
